{{Short description|American virologist, biologist, and molecular biologist (1936–2020)}}
'''Raymond Leo Erikson''' (January 24, 1936 – March 30, 2020) was a molecular biologist and virologist who noted research on cell growth and regulation.<ref name=":23">{{Cite news|last=Angier|first=Natalie|date=1990-11-06|title=Biologists Unravel Key Events of Cell Division|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/11/06/science/biologists-unravel-key-events-of-cell-division.html|access-date=2021-10-26|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He also served as the John F. Drum [[American Cancer Society]] Professor of Cellular and Developmental Biology at [[Harvard University]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Council|first1=National Research|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OzrmTzEOOnoC&pg=PA96|title=Research on Power-Frequency Fields Completed Under the Energy Policy Act of 1992|last2=Studies|first2=Division on Earth and Life|last3=Sciences|first3=Commission on Life|last4=of 1992|first4=Committee to Review the Research Activities Completed Under the Energy Policy Act|date=1999-07-07|publisher=National Academies Press|isbn=978-0-309-06543-6|language=en}}</ref>

== Childhood ==
Erikson was born in [[Eagle, Wisconsin]], on a dairy farm that was settled by his father and grandfather.<ref name=":23" /> Erikson was the oldest of two children.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal|last=Alcorta|first=David A.|date=2020-06-15|title=Raymond L. Erikson, PhD: In Memoriam (1936–2020)|url=https://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/80/12/2425|journal=Cancer Research|language=en|volume=80|issue=12|pages=2425–2426|doi=10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-20-1505|s2cid=219636614|issn=0008-5472|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Being from a small village, Erikson went to school in a one-room school house before going off to college.<ref name=":02" />

== Collegiate career ==
Erikson went to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin-Madison]] with the intent of being an [[agricultural science]]s teacher.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|date=2020-04-20|title=Ray Erikson 01.24.1936 – 03.30.2020|url=https://www.mcb.harvard.edu/department/news/ray-erikson-01-24-1936-03-30-2020/|access-date=2021-10-26|website=Harvard University - Department of Molecular & Cellular Biology|language=en-US}}</ref> It was not until his junior year where he gained interest in molecular biology after taking a course at college.<ref name=":13" /> After taking the course, Erikson developed a passion for molecular biology. In 1958, Erikson enrolled in the University of Wisconsin-Madison's graduate school where he worked with Dr. [[Wacław Szybalski|Waclaw Szybalski]].<ref name=":13" /> In 1963, Erikson had earned a [[Ph.D.]]

== Professional career ==
Upon completion of his Ph.D., Erikson moved out to Colorado and began pursuing a career in molecular biology research. Erikson spent a sabbatical (1972–1973) at the Imperial Cancer Research Fund Laboratories, where he became immersed in avian sarcoma virus-mediated transformation of cells. After his [[sabbatical]], in 1976 at the Richard M. Franklin at [[University of Colorado School of Medicine]], he researched [[RNA]] [[bacteriophage]]s.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal|last1=Blenis|first1=John|last2=Simmons|first2=Daniel L.|last3=Sweet|first3=Laurel|last4=Neel|first4=Benjamin G.|date=2020-06-18|title=Raymond L. Erikson (1936–2020)|journal=Molecular Cell|language=English|volume=78|issue=6|pages=988–990|doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2020.05.003|s2cid=225747795|issn=1097-2765|doi-access=free}}</ref> After focusing on [[RNA]] [[bacteriophage]]s, Erikson led a research team to begin research on the oncogene [[v-Src]].<ref name=":32" /> In 1977, Erikson and his research team had a breakthrough.<ref name=":32" /> One of the researchers was able to identify the [[protein]] associated with [[v-Src]]. This protein led to the determination of the pathway [[Src family kinase|Src]] uses to cause [[cancer]]. This pathway is considered to be one of the most important [[cancer]] promoting [[signal cascade]]s.<ref name=":13" /> The pathway was not the only discovery in this lab at the time. Another discovery was that the [[Src family kinase|Src]] was a threonine kinase. A standard methodology at the time was used in the lab to determine this [[Phosphoamino acid analysis|phosphoamino acid]].<ref name=":32" />

In 1982, Erikson decided to join the molecular and [[Cellular Biology|cellular biology]] department at [[Harvard University]].<ref name=":32" /> While at Harvard, Erikson was recognized for his contributions and discoveries about the v-Src [[oncogene]]. Some of the awards he earned included the [[Lasker Award]] (1982), the [[Robert Koch Prize]] (1982), the [[Alfred P. Sloan Prize|Alfred P. Sloan Award]] (1983), and the Hammer Prize for Cancer Research (1983).<ref name=":13" /> After finishing up his research of v-Src, Erikson encouraged his students to look into cell alterations such as morphology, motility and metabolism. One of these downstream alterations occurred in an ERK-MAP pathway. The alteration in this pathway was caused by a Ras oncogene. This discovery led to MEK inhibitors approved by the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] for [[Treatment of cancer|cancer treatment]].<ref name=":32" /> Another downstream alteration discovered was [[COX2]]. This pathway led to the inhibition of [[tyrosine kinase]]s.<ref name=":13" /> In cell cycle division, Erikson's lab focused on [[PLK1]] and saw that an increase in [[PLK1]] can lead to carcinogenic cells.<ref name=":32" /> Another aspect the lab focused on was [[RNA interference|RNAi]] and saw carcinogenic cells with [[RNA interference|RNAi]] present division decreased by 80%.<ref name=":32" /> Later in his career, Erikson served as the John F. Drum [[American Cancer Society]] Professor of Cellular and Developmental Biology.<ref name=":23" />

== Personal life ==
Erikson met his first wife Eleanor (Jo) Erikson while working in a lab under Dr. [[Wacław Szybalski|Waclaw Szybalski]].<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal|last=Alcorta|first=David A.|date=2020-06-15|title=Raymond L. Erikson, PhD: In Memoriam (1936–2020)|url=https://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/80/12/2425|journal=Cancer Research|language=en|volume=80|issue=12|pages=2425–2426|doi=10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-20-1505|s2cid=219636614|issn=0008-5472|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The two divorced after sometime. He later remarried to his second wife Donna. They were married for 32 years until his passing and had a daughter named Amanda.<ref name=":42" />
